source.text: Μικρὸν καὶ οὐκέτι θεωρεῖτέ με, καὶ πάλιν μικρὸν καὶ ὄψεσθέ με.

records.literal_gloss: A little and no longer you see me, and again a little and you will see me.

en.L: A little [while] and you no longer see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and again a little [while] and you will see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.
en.B: In a little while you will no longer see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and then after another little while you will see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.
en.R: In a little while you will not see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} anymore. Then a little while after that, you will see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} again.

fr.L: Un peu [de temps] et vous ne {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} voyez plus, et de nouveau un peu [de temps] et vous {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} verrez.
fr.B: Dans peu de temps, vous ne {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} verrez plus, puis, peu de temps après, vous {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} verrez.
fr.R: Dans peu de temps, vous ne {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} verrez plus. Puis, peu de temps après, vous {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} reverrez.

decisions.choice: two verbs for seeing, most likely for variety and because of the change of tense; both mean that the disciples will see Jesus
alternatives: the first verb means ordinary sight and the second a deeper seeing by faith
decisions.reason: The first "see" is θεωρεῖτέ (from θεωρέω), the second ὄψεσθέ, a future of ὁράω. The future of seeing was usually expressed with this second verb, so the change may simply follow the change of tense. John also uses the first verb for the disciples' seeing of Jesus after his death (14:19, "you see me"), so it does not stand only for bodily sight; and the second is used when the disciples see the risen Jesus (20:18, 20, 25, 29). Some readers find a contrast between seeing with the eyes and seeing with understanding, but John's usage does not clearly support it.

decisions.choice: the verse ends with "you will see me" (SBLGNT)
alternatives: adds "because I am going to the Father" (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The oldest manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, end the verse with "you will see me". Many later manuscripts add "because I am going to the Father", most likely taken from the disciples' question in verse 17, which joins this saying to the words of 16:10. A footnote gives the longer reading. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the two little whiles: first the short time until Jesus's death, then the short time until the disciples see him risen
alternatives: the second little while ends with the coming of the Spirit (14:16-19; 16:7)
the second little while ends with Jesus's return at the end of the age (14:3)
decisions.reason: Jesus is speaking on the night before his death, so the first little while is a matter of hours. The second ends when they see him again, and verses 20-22 describe that seeing as sorrow turned to joy; John tells it in those terms when the risen Jesus comes to them: "the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord" (20:20). In 14:18-19 the same words about seeing him are tied to his coming to them and to the gift of the Spirit, and the promised joy and asking in his name (16:22-24) reach beyond Easter into the life of the church, so some take the second little while of the Spirit's coming or of his final return. The Easter reading fits the closest words best, but the others cannot be ruled out.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ or for God uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "me" and "my" when Jesus speaks of himself, "he" and "his" when the disciples or the narrator speak of him, and "he" for the Father. At the start of a sentence "He" or "My" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: In a little while ... after another little while (B); In a little while ... a little while after that ... again (R); "will no longer see" in the future
alternatives: In a short time (as Balanced has in 14:19)
decisions.reason: In 14:19 Balanced and Readable say "in a short time" and "soon". Here they keep "a little while", because the disciples puzzle over that very phrase in verses 17-19 ("What is this 'little while'?"), and the same words must recur. The present "you no longer see" speaks of what is about to happen, so Balanced and Readable put it in the future, as in 14:19. Readable adds "again" to the second clause, which "again a little while" implies.

decisions.choice: un peu [de temps] (L); Dans peu de temps ... peu de temps après (B, R)
alternatives: Encore un peu de temps ... et encore un peu de temps
decisions.reason: French "un peu" alone does not name a stretch of time, so Literal brackets "de temps". Balanced and Readable put the first "little while" in the future, as the English does, and keep the words "peu de temps" at both points (meaning decision m3), because the disciples quote the saying in verses 17 and 19 and puzzle over "peu de temps" in verse 18; every level repeats its own wording there.

source.text: εἶπαν οὖν ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ πρὸς ἀλλήλους· Τί ἐστιν τοῦτο ὃ λέγει ἡμῖν· Μικρὸν καὶ οὐ θεωρεῖτέ με, καὶ πάλιν μικρὸν καὶ ὄψεσθέ με;

records.literal_gloss: Said therefore [some] of the disciples of him to one another, "What is this that he says to us, 'A little and not you see me, and again a little and you will see me';

en.L: So [some] of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples said to one another, "What is this that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says to us, 'A little [while] and you do not see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and again a little [while] and you will see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}'?
en.B: Then some of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples said to one another, "What does {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} mean by telling us, 'In a little while you will no longer see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and then after another little while you will see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}'?
en.R: Some of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples began asking each other, "What does {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} mean by saying, 'In a little while you will not see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} anymore. Then a little while after that, you will see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} again'?

fr.L: [Certains] de {{deity_pronoun:ses|Ses}} disciples se dirent donc les uns aux autres : « Qu’est-ce que cela, ce qu’{{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} nous dit : “Un peu [de temps] et vous ne {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} voyez pas, et de nouveau un peu [de temps] et vous {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} verrez” ?
fr.B: Alors quelques-uns de {{deity_pronoun:ses|Ses}} disciples se dirent entre eux : « Que veut-{{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} dire en nous disant : “Dans peu de temps, vous ne {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} verrez plus, puis, peu de temps après, vous {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} verrez” ?
fr.R: Quelques-uns de {{deity_pronoun:ses|Ses}} disciples ont commencé à se demander entre eux : « Que veut-{{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} dire quand {{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} dit : “Dans peu de temps, vous ne {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} verrez plus. Puis, peu de temps après, vous {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} reverrez” ?

decisions.choice: some of his disciples, not all of them
decisions.reason: The phrase "out of his disciples" (ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν) has no word for "some"; the preposition itself marks a part of the group, as in 7:40. They speak "to one another", not to Jesus: they want to ask him but hold back (verse 19; compare 16:5).

decisions.choice: the disciples repeat Jesus's saying of verse 16 word for word, with one small change that does not alter its sense
decisions.reason: In verse 16 Jesus said "no longer" (οὐκέτι); the disciples, and Jesus himself in verse 19, say simply "not" (οὐ). The rest is the same. The saying is repeated three times in four verses (16, 17, 19), which shows how much it puzzled them and fixes it in the reader's mind.

decisions.choice: the disciples cannot yet understand that Jesus speaks of his death and resurrection
decisions.reason: John often notes that the disciples understood Jesus's words only after he rose (2:22; 12:16; 20:9). Here their question shows the same thing from the inside: they hear the words but cannot see what event they point to.

decisions.choice: the quotation repeats the wording of verse 16 at Balanced and Readable; Literal has "you do not see" for the one changed word
decisions.reason: The disciples quote what Jesus has just said, so Balanced and Readable repeat verse 16 exactly, as the reader will recognise it. Literal shows the one word that changes (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable turn "What is this that he says" into "What does he mean", the natural English for asking about the sense of words.

decisions.choice: narration in the passé simple (L, B; "se dirent", "dit"), with the imperfect for what went on ("disaient"); passé composé (R; "ont commencé", "a dit"); speech in the passé composé at every level
alternatives: passé composé for narration at every level
decisions.reason: The French brief for the passage (16:16-24), as in 1:19. The passé simple is the normal tense of written narrative and suits a public reading; Readable uses the passé composé, the past tense French readers speak and learn first. Inside Jesus's words every level uses the passé composé ("j’ai dit", "vous n’avez rien demandé"). This passage has no historic present.

source.text: καί· Ὅτι ὑπάγω πρὸς τὸν πατέρα;

records.literal_gloss: and, "Because I go to the Father"?"

en.L: And, 'Because I am going to the Father'?"
en.B: And what about 'because I am going to the Father'?"
en.R: And what does {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} mean, 'because I am going to the Father'?"

fr.L: Et : “Parce que je vais vers le Père” ? »
fr.B: Et que veut dire : “parce que je vais vers le Père” ? »
fr.R: Et que veut-{{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} dire par : “parce que je vais vers le Père” ? »

decisions.choice: Ὅτι here means "because": the disciples quote Jesus's words of 16:10
alternatives: the word only introduces the quotation ("and, 'I am going to the Father'")
decisions.reason: This word often simply opens a quotation, and that is possible here. But 16:10 has the same words, "because I am going to the Father", and the disciples are putting together things Jesus has said in this discourse; they quote that phrase as he said it, reason word and all.

decisions.choice: going to the Father: Jesus's return to the Father through his death, resurrection and exaltation
decisions.reason: Jesus has spoken of his going to the Father again and again (13:1; 14:12, 28; 16:5, 10, 28). The disciples put this saying beside the one about the little while and cannot see how the two fit: how can he go away to the Father and also be seen again?

decisions.choice: And what about ... (B); And what does he mean, ... (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek has only "and" before the second quoted saying; the question "What is this?" carries over from the first part. Balanced and Readable supply "what about" and "what does he mean" so that the second saying is plainly a second question.

source.text: ἔλεγον οὖν· Τί ἐστιν τοῦτο ὃ λέγει μικρόν;

records.literal_gloss: They were saying therefore, "What is this that he says, 'little'?

en.L: So they were saying, "What is this that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, 'a little [while]'?
en.B: So they kept saying, "What does {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} mean by 'a little while'?
en.R: They kept asking, "What does {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} mean by 'a little while'?

fr.L: Ils disaient donc : « Qu’est-ce que ce “un peu [de temps]” qu’{{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} dit ?
fr.B: Ils répétaient donc : « Que veut-{{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} dire par “peu de temps” ?
fr.R: Ils n’arrêtaient pas de se demander : « Que veut-{{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} dire par “peu de temps” ?

decisions.choice: they were saying: they talked it over again and again
decisions.reason: The verb ἔλεγον is imperfect, the tense of continued or repeated action: the question went round among them.

decisions.choice: "little while" is what puzzles them most
decisions.reason: Of everything Jesus has said, they single out the phrase "a little while". They cannot tell what span of time he means, or what will happen at its end.

decisions.choice: kept saying (B); kept asking (R)
decisions.reason: "Kept saying" gives the sense of the continuing tense (meaning decision m1) in plain English. Readable says "asking", since what they say is a question.

records.literal_gloss: Not we know what he speaks."

en.L: We do not know what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is speaking [of]."
en.B: We do not understand what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is talking about."
en.R: We do not understand what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is talking about."

fr.L: Nous ne savons pas ce qu’{{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} dit. »
fr.B: Nous ne comprenons pas de quoi {{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} parle. »
fr.R: Nous ne comprenons pas ce qu’{{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} veut dire. »

decisions.choice: we do not know what he is speaking of: they cannot grasp his meaning
decisions.reason: They have heard the words; what they lack is their meaning. "Know" (οἴδαμεν) here is understanding, as when Jesus says that his disciples did not understand his words until later (13:7). Jesus will soon speak to them plainly (16:25, 29).

decisions.choice: do not understand
decisions.reason: In English "we do not know what he is talking about" can sound dismissive; "understand" says that they are puzzled, which is the sense (meaning decision m1).

source.text: ἔγνω Ἰησοῦς ὅτι ἤθελον αὐτὸν ἐρωτᾶν, καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Περὶ τούτου ζητεῖτε μετ’ ἀλλήλων ὅτι εἶπον· Μικρὸν καὶ οὐ θεωρεῖτέ με, καὶ πάλιν μικρὸν καὶ ὄψεσθέ με;

records.literal_gloss: Knew Jesus that they were wanting him to ask, and he said to them, "About this are you seeking with one another, that I said, 'A little and not you see me, and again a little and you will see me'?"

en.L: Jesus knew that they wanted to ask {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "Are you inquiring with one another about this, that I said, 'A little [while] and you do not see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and again a little [while] and you will see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}'?"
en.B: Jesus knew that they wanted to ask {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} about it, so {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "Are you discussing with one another what I meant when I said, 'In a little while you will no longer see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and then after another little while you will see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}'?"
en.R: Jesus knew that they wanted to ask {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} about this. So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "Are you asking each other what I meant by these words: 'In a little while you will not see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} anymore. Then a little while after that, you will see {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} again'?"

fr.L: Jésus sut qu’ils voulaient {{deity_pronoun:l’|L’}}interroger, et {{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} leur dit : « Est-ce à ce sujet que vous vous interrogez les uns les autres, parce que j’ai dit : “Un peu [de temps] et vous ne {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} voyez pas, et de nouveau un peu [de temps] et vous {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} verrez” ? »
fr.B: Jésus savait qu’ils voulaient {{deity_pronoun:l’|L’}}interroger à ce sujet ; {{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} leur dit donc : « Vous discutez entre vous de ce que j’ai voulu dire par : “Dans peu de temps, vous ne {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} verrez plus, puis, peu de temps après, vous {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} verrez” ? »
fr.R: Jésus savait qu’ils voulaient {{deity_pronoun:l’|L’}}interroger là-dessus. Alors {{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} leur a dit : « Vous vous demandez entre vous ce que j’ai voulu dire par ces mots : “Dans peu de temps, vous ne {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} verrez plus. Puis, peu de temps après, vous {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} reverrez” ? »

decisions.choice: Jesus knew: he was aware of their wish before they spoke; John does not say how
alternatives: he noticed it from their talk among themselves
decisions.reason: Jesus may simply have seen them talking together. But John often says that Jesus knew what was in people (2:24-25; 6:61, 64; 13:11), and a few verses later the disciples say, "Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you" (16:30), which answers this very moment. John most likely means more than ordinary noticing, though the words alone do not say so.

decisions.choice: ask him: put a question to him; seeking with one another: discussing among themselves
decisions.reason: The verb for "ask" (ἐρωτᾶν, from ἐρωτάω) is the one for asking a question, and it returns in verse 23: "in that day you will ask me nothing". The verb ζητεῖτε means seeking, here seeking an answer together, talking it over.

decisions.choice: Jesus repeats his saying in the same words as the disciples did
decisions.reason: Jesus quotes himself with "not" instead of "no longer", exactly as the disciples did in verse 17. He does not explain the riddle directly; he answers with what the little whiles will bring: sorrow and then joy (verses 20-22).

decisions.choice: discussing with one another what I meant when I said (B); asking each other what I meant by these words (R); the quoted saying as in verse 16
alternatives: inquiring with one another about this, that I said (Literal)
decisions.reason: "About this ... that I said" is a Greek way of pointing to the words in question; Balanced says "what I meant when I said", Readable "what I meant by these words". The quoted saying is worded as in verse 16 so that readers recognise it.

source.text: ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι κλαύσετε καὶ θρηνήσετε ὑμεῖς, ὁ δὲ κόσμος χαρήσεται· ὑμεῖς λυπηθήσεσθε, ἀλλ’ ἡ λύπη ὑμῶν εἰς χαρὰν γενήσεται.

records.literal_gloss: Truly truly I say to you that will weep and will lament you, the but world will rejoice; you will be grieved, but the grief of you into joy will become.

en.L: Truly, truly I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be made sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy.
en.B: Truly, truly, I tell you, you will weep and mourn aloud, but the world will rejoice. You will be full of sorrow, but your sorrow will become joy.
en.R: I tell you the truth: you will cry and mourn, but the world will be glad. You will be very sad, but your sadness will turn into joy.

fr.L: En vérité, en vérité, je vous le dis, vous pleurerez et vous vous lamenterez, vous, mais le monde se réjouira ; vous serez peinés, mais votre peine deviendra joie.
fr.B: En vérité, en vérité, je vous le dis : vous pleurerez et vous vous lamenterez à grands cris, mais le monde se réjouira. Vous serez dans la peine, mais votre peine se transformera en joie.
fr.R: Je vous le dis, c’est la vérité : vous allez pleurer et vous lamenter, mais le monde, lui, se réjouira. Vous serez très tristes, mais votre tristesse se transformera en joie.

decisions.choice: weep and lament: loud mourning, the kind made for the dead
decisions.reason: "Weep" (κλαύσετε) is crying aloud, as Mary and the mourners wept for Lazarus (11:31, 33). "Lament" (θρηνήσετε) is the wailing of a funeral; Luke uses it of the women who mourned for Jesus on the way to the cross (Luke 23:27). Jesus is telling them that they will mourn him as one who has died.

decisions.choice: the world: humanity set against Jesus, which will be glad at his death
decisions.reason: As in 15:18-19, the world is set against the disciples: those who hate Jesus and want him gone. The stressed "you" and "the world" are put side by side: the same event will bring grief to one and gladness to the other.

decisions.choice: your sorrow will become joy: the same events that cause their grief will become the cause of their joy
alternatives: their sorrow will be replaced by joy
decisions.reason: The Greek says that the sorrow itself "will become" joy, not that joy will come after it. The death they mourn, once he is risen, becomes the ground of their joy. Verse 21 gives a picture of exactly this: the pain of childbirth issues in the joy of a new life.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage; it applies also in verse 23.

decisions.choice: weep and lament (L); weep and mourn aloud (B); cry and mourn (R); sorrow (L, B) and sadness (R) for the noun throughout verses 20-22
decisions.reason: Balanced says "mourn aloud" for the loud lament of mourners (meaning decision m1). The noun for sorrow occurs in verses 20, 21 and 22, and the link between them is the point of the picture, so Literal and Balanced say "sorrow" each time and Readable says "sad" or "sadness" in verses 20 and 22.

decisions.choice: En vérité, en vérité, je vous le dis (L, B); Je vous le dis, c’est la vérité (R)
alternatives: Amen, amen, je vous le dis
Oui, vraiment, je vous le dis
decisions.reason: The book-wide French rendering for John, recorded once in this passage (16:20, 23). Readable puts the pledge in plain words.

decisions.choice: peinés, la peine (L, B); tristes, la tristesse (R), and "souffrir", "la douleur" for the woman in labour (R, verse 21)
decisions.reason: The same noun runs through verses 20-22, for the disciples' grief and for the pain of labour (verse 21, meaning decision m1 there). French "la peine" covers both grief and hardship, so Literal and Balanced can keep one word for both, where "tristesse" would sound odd for a woman giving birth. Readable uses the plainest word in each place, as the English Readable does.

source.text: ἡ γυνὴ ὅταν τίκτῃ λύπην ἔχει, ὅτι ἦλθεν ἡ ὥρα αὐτῆς· ὅταν δὲ γεννήσῃ τὸ παιδίον, οὐκέτι μνημονεύει τῆς θλίψεως διὰ τὴν χαρὰν ὅτι ἐγεννήθη ἄνθρωπος εἰς τὸν κόσμον.

records.literal_gloss: The woman when she gives birth sorrow has, because came the hour of her; when but she has borne the child, no longer she remembers the affliction because of the joy that was born a human being into the world.

en.L: The woman, when she is giving birth, has sorrow, because her hour has come; but when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers the anguish, because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world.
en.B: When a woman is giving birth she has sorrow, because her hour has come. But once her child is born, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world.
en.R: When a woman is having a baby, she is in pain, because her time has come. But after the baby is born, she forgets all that pain. She is full of joy that a new person has come into the world.

fr.L: La femme, lorsqu’elle enfante, a de la peine, parce que son heure est venue ; mais lorsqu’elle a mis au monde l’enfant, elle ne se souvient plus de la détresse, à cause de la joie de ce qu’un être humain est né dans le monde.
fr.B: Quand une femme accouche, elle est dans la peine, parce que son heure est venue. Mais une fois l’enfant né, elle ne se souvient plus de ses souffrances, tant elle a de joie qu’un être humain soit venu au monde.
fr.R: Quand une femme met un bébé au monde, elle souffre, parce que le moment est venu. Mais quand le bébé est né, elle oublie toute sa douleur. Elle est pleine de joie parce qu’un nouvel être humain est venu au monde.

decisions.choice: sorrow: the pain and distress of labor, called by the same word as the disciples' sorrow
decisions.reason: The noun λύπην usually means grief, but it is also used of bodily pain, and here it covers both. Jesus uses the same word for the disciples in verses 20 and 22, so that the woman's labor is a picture of their grief.

decisions.choice: her hour: the time for her child to be born
alternatives: a deliberate echo of Jesus's own hour
decisions.reason: In the picture, "her hour" is simply the time of giving birth. Yet "the hour" is John's word for the time of Jesus's death and glory (12:23, 27; 13:1; 17:1), and the woman's hour stands for the disciples' hour of grief at that death. The plain sense is certain; how far John means the echo is not.

decisions.choice: ἄνθρωπος: a human being, a new person
decisions.reason: The word is the general word for a human being, not the word for a male. The point is not the child's sex but that a new human life has come into the world, which outweighs the pain.

decisions.choice: the pains of childbirth: a picture the prophets used for the distress that comes before God's new age
alternatives: an everyday picture with no particular passage in view
decisions.reason: The prophets compare Israel's suffering before God saves it to a woman in labor (Isaiah 26:17-19, where the picture ends in the dead rising; 66:7-14; Micah 4:9-10). Isaiah 66 also gives the words Jesus uses in verse 22 (66:14, "you will see, and your heart will rejoice"). The picture works on its own as everyday life; that John wants readers to hear the prophets as well is likely but not certain.

decisions.choice: sorrow (L, B), pain (R); anguish (L, B), all that pain (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "sorrow" for the same noun as in verses 20 and 22, so the link stays visible (meaning decision m1). Readable says "pain", which a young reader expects of childbirth. For the second noun, a word for pressure and distress, Literal and Balanced say "anguish".

decisions.choice: a woman (B, R); her hour (L, B), her time (R); a human being (L, B), a new person (R)
decisions.reason: The article with "woman" marks the general case, so Balanced and Readable say "a woman". Literal and Balanced keep "her hour" so that the echo of Jesus's hour can be heard (meaning decision m2); Readable says "her time". "A human being" is already inclusive, so no setting is needed; "a man" would suggest a male child, which the word does not mean (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: un être humain (L, B); un nouvel être humain (R)
decisions.reason: The word means a human being, not a male child (meaning decision m3). French "un homme" would now be read as "a man", so every level says "être humain"; this is the plain meaning, not a reader setting.

source.text: καὶ ὑμεῖς οὖν νῦν μὲν λύπην ἔχετε· πάλιν δὲ ὄψομαι ὑμᾶς, καὶ χαρήσεται ὑμῶν ἡ καρδία, καὶ τὴν χαρὰν ὑμῶν οὐδεὶς αἴρει ἀφ’ ὑμῶν.

records.literal_gloss: And you therefore now indeed sorrow have; again but I will see you, and will rejoice of you the heart, and the joy of you no one takes from you.

en.L: So you also now have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and your joy no one takes from you.
en.B: So it is with you: now you have sorrow, but I will see you again. Then your hearts will rejoice, and no one takes your joy away from you.
en.R: It is the same for you. You are sad now. But I will see you again. Then your hearts will be full of gladness. No one will ever take your joy away from you.

fr.L: Vous aussi donc, maintenant, vous avez de la peine ; mais je vous verrai de nouveau, et votre cœur se réjouira, et votre joie, personne ne vous l’enlève.
fr.B: Il en est de même pour vous : maintenant vous êtes dans la peine, mais je vous reverrai. Alors vos cœurs se réjouiront, et votre joie, personne ne vous l’enlève.
fr.R: C’est pareil pour vous. Maintenant, vous êtes tristes. Mais je vous reverrai. Alors vos cœurs seront remplis de joie. Et personne ne pourra jamais vous enlever votre joie.

decisions.choice: I will see you again: Jesus will come to them risen, and their grief will turn to gladness
decisions.reason: In verse 16 the disciples are the ones who will see; here Jesus is: he will come and see them. This happens on the evening of the resurrection, when he stands among them and "the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord" (20:19-20).

decisions.choice: your heart will rejoice: the words of Isaiah 66:14
decisions.reason: Isaiah 66 pictures Zion giving birth suddenly to a new people (66:7-9) and then says, "you will see, and your heart will rejoice" (66:14); the Greek translation of Isaiah has the same words as here. The labor picture of verse 21 and this promise come together from the same chapter. A reviewer should check the wording against the Greek of Isaiah.

decisions.choice: no one takes, present (αἴρει, SBLGNT)
alternatives: no one will take, future (some early manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Some early manuscripts have the future, "no one will take". The SBLGNT reads the present. The sense is nearly the same: the present states it as a settled fact. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: no one takes your joy: a joy beyond anyone's reach, from then on
decisions.reason: The present states what will always be so: unlike their sorrow, which lasts only a little while, the joy of seeing him again cannot be taken from them by the world or anyone else. "Your heart" is singular, the heart of each and of all together.

decisions.choice: your hearts (B, R); no one takes ... away (B); No one will ever take ... away (R); full of gladness (R)
decisions.reason: English says "hearts" for the heart of each of several people. Balanced keeps the present "takes", which in English can state a lasting fact; Readable says "will ever take" to make the lasting fact plain (meaning decision m4). Readable says "full of gladness" for the verb "rejoice", keeping "joy" for the noun.

source.text: καὶ ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐμὲ οὐκ ἐρωτήσετε οὐδέν· ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ἄν τι αἰτήσητε τὸν πατέρα δώσει ὑμῖν ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου.

records.literal_gloss: And in that the day me not you will ask nothing; truly truly I say to you, if anything you ask the Father he will give to you in the name of me.

en.L: And in that day you will ask {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} nothing. Truly, truly I say to you, if you ask the Father anything, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will give [it] to you in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name.
en.B: On that day you will not ask {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} any questions. Truly, truly, I tell you, if you ask the Father for anything, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will give it to you in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name.
en.R: When that day comes, you will have no more questions to ask {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. I tell you the truth: if you ask the Father for anything, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will give it to you in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name.

fr.L: Et en ce jour-là, vous ne {{deity_pronoun:m’|M’}}interrogerez sur rien. En vérité, en vérité, je vous le dis, si vous demandez quelque chose au Père, {{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} vous [le] donnera en {{deity_pronoun:mon|Mon}} nom.
fr.B: Ce jour-là, vous ne {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} poserez aucune question. En vérité, en vérité, je vous le dis : si vous demandez quoi que ce soit au Père, {{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} vous le donnera en {{deity_pronoun:mon|Mon}} nom.
fr.R: Quand ce jour-là viendra, vous n’aurez plus de questions à {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} poser. Je vous le dis, c’est la vérité : si vous demandez quelque chose au Père, {{deity_pronoun:il|Il}} vous le donnera en {{deity_pronoun:mon|Mon}} nom.

decisions.choice: two verbs for asking: "ask me nothing" (ἐρωτήσετε) means asking questions; "ask the Father" (αἰτήσητε) means asking for something
alternatives: both mean making requests: in that day they will not make requests of Jesus but of the Father
decisions.reason: The first verb is the one used in verse 19, where the disciples wanted to question Jesus, and in 16:5 and 16:30 for questioning him. The second is the ordinary verb for asking for something, the one used for prayer in 14:13-14, 15:7, 16 and verse 24. So Jesus most likely means: in that day you will have no more questions for me, and whatever you ask for, the Father will give. But the first verb can also mean a request (14:16; 16:26), and some take both halves to be about prayer.

decisions.choice: in that day: the time after Jesus is raised, when they see him again and the Spirit teaches them
decisions.reason: "That day" (14:20) is the time that begins when he comes to them again (verse 22). Then the Spirit will guide them into all the truth (16:13; 14:26), and Jesus will speak to them plainly about the Father (16:25); their puzzled questions of verses 17-19 will be answered.

decisions.choice: he will give you in my name (SBLGNT): "in my name" goes with the giving
alternatives: whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you (many manuscripts)
decisions.reason: In the SBLGNT, supported by some of the oldest manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, "in my name" comes after "he will give you": the Father gives in Jesus's name. Many other manuscripts, among them Codex Alexandrinus and most later ones, put "in my name" before "he will give you", so that it is the asking that is done in his name, as in 14:13-14, 15:16 and verse 24. The difference is real but small, since both the asking and the giving rest on Jesus. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: he will give in my name: the Father gives for Jesus's sake and through him
decisions.reason: A name stands for the person (see 14:13). The Father's gifts come to the disciples on account of Jesus and through him; the next verse adds that they are to ask in his name too. Asking and giving both rest on him.

decisions.choice: you will not ask me any questions (B); you will have no more questions to ask me (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that the first "ask" is about questions (meaning decision m1), so that it is not confused with asking the Father for things in the next sentence. Readable's "no more" connects the promise to the puzzled questions of verses 17-19. Literal keeps the same word "ask" for both verbs. "Truly, truly" is rendered as in verse 20.

decisions.choice: interroger, poser des questions (asking Jesus); demander (asking the Father)
decisions.reason: Greek uses two verbs here (meaning decision m1): one for asking questions, one for asking for something. French "demander" alone would blur them, so the first is "interroger" (L) or "poser des questions" (B, R) and the second "demander".

source.text: ἕως ἄρτι οὐκ ᾐτήσατε οὐδὲν ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου· αἰτεῖτε καὶ λήμψεσθε, ἵνα ἡ χαρὰ ὑμῶν ᾖ πεπληρωμένη.

records.literal_gloss: Until now not you asked nothing in the name of me; ask and you will receive, so that the joy of you may be having been made full.

en.L: Until now you have asked nothing in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name; ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be made full.
en.B: So far you have asked for nothing in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name. Ask and you will receive, so that your joy will be complete.
en.R: Up to now you have never asked for anything in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name. Keep asking, and you will receive, so that your joy will be full.

fr.L: Jusqu’à maintenant, vous n’avez rien demandé en {{deity_pronoun:mon|Mon}} nom ; demandez et vous recevrez, afin que votre joie soit rendue pleine.
fr.B: Jusqu’ici, vous n’avez rien demandé en {{deity_pronoun:mon|Mon}} nom. Demandez, et vous recevrez, pour que votre joie soit complète.
fr.R: Jusqu’à maintenant, vous n’avez jamais rien demandé en {{deity_pronoun:mon|Mon}} nom. Demandez, et demandez encore : vous recevrez, et ainsi votre joie sera pleine.

decisions.choice: until now: while Jesus was with them they asked him directly; asking in his name belongs to the time after he goes to the Father
decisions.reason: During his ministry the disciples brought their needs to Jesus himself. Asking the Father in Jesus's name is new: it belongs to the time when he has gone to the Father (14:12-14; 15:16; 16:26). "In my name" means asking as those who belong to him, on the ground of who he is (see 14:13).

decisions.choice: ask and you will receive: a standing invitation to keep asking
decisions.reason: The command "ask" (αἰτεῖτε) is in the present tense, which suits a continuing practice: go on asking. The promise "you will receive" answers it, as in Matthew 7:7-8.

decisions.choice: so that your joy may be complete: the same joy Jesus promised in 15:11
decisions.reason: "Made full" (πεπληρωμένη) is the verb of 15:11 and 17:13, here in a perfect form: a joy filled and staying full. Answered prayer is one way the joy of verse 22 is made complete.

decisions.choice: your joy may be made full (L); your joy will be complete (B); your joy will be full (R)
decisions.reason: The same wording as 15:11 at each level, since Jesus repeats that promise here. "Joy" is the key term at every level. Readable says "Keep asking" for the present-tense command (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: Demandez, et demandez encore
decisions.reason: The present imperative is a standing invitation (meaning decision m2). The English Readable says "Keep asking", but "continuez à demander" would imply they have been asking in his name already, which verse 24a denies; repeating the verb keeps the sense of going on asking.
